title: Name your feelings, trace the chain, know your triggers

say: Name your feelings, trace the chain, and know your triggers.
This is the video for module one of Emotional Intelligence for Daily Life.
Emotional intelligence, often called EI or EQ, is the ability to notice emotions in yourself and in other people.

panel.heading: Emotional intelligence in plain words
items: Notice emotions in yourself and others
Understand what they are telling you
Use that to guide what you say and do
A skill you can learn, like sewing

say: It means understanding what those feelings are telling you, and using that to guide what you say and do.
It is not about never getting angry. It is about handling feelings so they help you instead of controlling you.

panel.heading: Emotional intelligence in plain words
items: Notice emotions in yourself and others
Understand what they are telling you
Use that to guide what you say and do
A skill you can learn, like sewing

say: And it is a skill. Like learning to drive or to sew, it improves with practice.

say: For example, Ngozi runs a provisions shop in Onitsha. One morning the generator will not start, the children are late, and a supplier says her goods will come two days late.
Without EI, she shouts at her son and snaps at the supplier.

panel.heading: Ngozi's hard morning, with EI
items: Perceive: my jaw is tight, my voice is rising
Understand: three things went wrong at once
Manage: three slow breaths, calm words
Use: the urgency pushes her to find a backup

say: With EI, she first perceives. She notices her jaw is tight and her voice is rising.

panel.heading: Ngozi's hard morning, with EI

Understand: three things went wrong at once

say: She understands. She tells herself, I am stressed because three things went wrong at once, not because my son is bad.

panel.heading: Ngozi's hard morning, with EI
items: Perceive: my jaw is tight, my voice is rising
Understand: three things went wrong at once
Manage: three slow breaths, calm words
Use: the urgency pushes her to find a backup

say: She manages. She takes three slow breaths, asks her son to help his sisters, and calmly asks the supplier for a firm new date by 12 noon.

panel.heading: Ngozi's hard morning, with EI
items: Perceive: my jaw is tight, my voice is rising

say: And she uses the feeling. The push of urgency gets her to call a second supplier as a backup. Same problems, but her relationships are protected.

say: If you cannot name what you feel, you cannot manage it. Putting a feeling into words helps calm it. Some call this name it to tame it.
The Mood Meter asks two questions. How much energy do I have? And how pleasant does this feel?

panel.heading: The Mood Meter: four zones
items: Red: high energy, unpleasant. Angry, anxious
Yellow: high energy, pleasant. Excited, proud
Blue: low energy, unpleasant. Sad, lonely
Green: low energy, pleasant. Calm, grateful

say: Red is high energy and unpleasant: angry, anxious, frustrated.

No zone is bad. For example, Aisha, a teacher, said she was just tired. Looking closer, she found the exact words: humiliated and discouraged. Now she knew what she needed.

say: Emotions follow a chain. Something happens, and you add a thought about what it means.
For example, Funmi posts photos of her new tailoring shop on the family WhatsApp group. Two hours later, only her aunt has replied. She thinks, nobody supports me.

panel.heading: How a feeling becomes an action
items: Situation happens
Thought or interpretation
Feeling and body response
Urge to act
Action and result

say: She feels hurt, and her body wants to act. The urge is to leave the group.

say: But an urge is not an order. She checks the evidence. It is a weekday afternoon, and most cousins are at work.
She stays in the group and sends the photos to two cousins directly. By evening she has 9 replies and one cousin has booked a fitting.

panel.rule: An urge is not an order. Widen the gap, then choose.

say: Some thoughts pour fuel on the fire. Mind-reading, always and never, imagining the worst, and calling yourself names.

panel.heading: Fuel thoughts, and three questions
left: She thinks I am a failure
right: What would I tell a friend?

say: When you notice one, ask three questions. What is the evidence? What else could explain this? What would I tell a friend who thought this?
This is not pretending everything is fine. If someone really treats you badly, see it clearly and respond wisely.

say: A trigger is anything that sets off a reaction bigger than the situation deserves. For example, Blessing sells foodstuff in Port Harcourt. She logs every strong reaction for one week.

panel.heading: Blessing's trigger log
items: Log every strong reaction for a week
6 of 11 came before 10am
5 of those 6: she was hungry
Plan: eat first, a sign for credit
Next week: 5 reactions, not 11

say: 6 of her 11 reactions happened before 10am, and 5 of those 6 were marked hungry.

panel.heading: Blessing's trigger log
items: Log every strong reaction for a week
6 of 11 came before 10am
5 of those 6: she was hungry
Plan: eat first, a sign for credit
Next week: 5 reactions, not 11

say: That is the HALT check. Am I hungry, angry, lonely or tired? Any of these makes small problems feel bigger.

say: To remember. EI is a skill you can practise. Find your zone, then the exact word. The chain can be interrupted. Use HALT and a trigger log.

This course is not therapy. If low mood, worry or anger lasts for weeks, or you have thoughts of harming yourself or others, please speak to a health professional, a trusted faith leader or the nearest hospital.
